newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: U.S. Democrats divided on hi-tech arms for Latam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Democrats divided on hi-tech arms for Latam.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt said on Friday he saw majority support for President Bill Clinton's decision to lift a ban on hi-tech arms sales to Latin America.

But Democratic Rep. Patrick Kennedy of Rhode Island, accompanying Gephardt on a fact-finding Latin American tour, warned that scrapping the 20-year ban imposed by the Carter administration would send the wrong signals about U.S. arms policy.
"I feel the pressure on us to sell arms will increase. And because it is the U.S. that is selling weapons, it gives impression that it is okay to keep buying," Kennedy said.

The U.S. Democrats were on a fact-finding tour of Chile, Argentina and Brazil ahead of Clinton's Latin American tour in October. Gephardt said their aim was to gauge opinion on "economy, trade, defense and foreign policy issues."
Clinton gave U.S. arms manufacturers a major boost on Aug. 1 when he scrapped the weapons ban imposed when much of Latin America was under brutal military rule.

Lobbying efforts by U.S. producers, coupled with Latin American interest in European sources for fighter jets, helped to hasten the end of the ban, despite concerns it could spark an arms race in the newly democratic but still poor region.
Gephardt acknowledged that Congress was divided over Latin American arms sales but "majority opinion is to approve it."

"I don't believe there is any intention of any sort of arms competition and some countries are in genuine need to modernize their forces," he told reporters after meeting Argentine government officials.

U.S. officials have said they plan to hand Argentine President Carlos Menem a major diplomatic coup by giving the country special status as major non-NATO U.S. ally in recognition of Argentine participation in U.N. peace missions and its military support in the 1991 Gulf War.
Gephardt said this would allow Argentina's armed forces, whose budget and powers have been slashed since democracy returned in 1983, priority to buy Pentagon war materiel.
"It is important for Argentina to have access to military goods that we have, that we can make available at a reasonable price to help both countries continue with these efforts," he said.
But Kennedy also disagreed on the new status, warning that it could create envy and regional tensions in Latin America.

"I have just come from Chile and I don't think we fully appreciated the impact on neighboring countries," he said, adding that selective arms sales and special status "could be in the future the opportunity for some schism."

Chile is likely to become the first Latin American nation to benefit from the lifting of the arms ban. U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has signaled that Washington would look favorably on the sale to Chile of U.S.-made F-16 jets.

But Kennedy said special U.S. status for Argentina, with which Chile has a long history of border disputes, made Chile "upset in some way because they interpret our relationship with Argentina as a rejection -- even though it is not."
